issues.title: Discord: an auto-thread whose create response was lost drops the user's message
issues.body:
Split out of #34611. #34649 ships only the message-create half: it stops re-sending a message create that may have landed.

## What happens

`create_thread_from_message` (`src/kiro_crew/discord/client.py`) POSTs `/channels/{c}/messages/{m}/threads` through the REST ladder, which retries it after a timeout or a 5xx.

1. The first attempt creates the thread, but its response is lost.
2. The retry is refused with code 160004 ("a thread has already been created for this message"). That is a permanent 4xx, so `_api` returns `None`.
3. `DiscordTransport.receive` logs `thread_create_failed` and never dispatches the user's message.

The thread exists in the server, but the user gets no reply.

## Why it was deferred

A recovery that adopts the existing thread (at the message's own id, via `thread_origin`, opener = this bot, same parent) reverses a "failed" answer into a grant. CI's GPT lane kept finding admission edges that such a grant has to re-check:

- a refusal while a retry waits
- a foreign opener
- a sender or channel withdrawn during the lookup
- a thread revoked during the lookup

Any fix should go through one admission path rather than a second one in the client. For example, have `receive` route an adopted id through `readmit_own_thread`, which already reads the rosters and `_revoked_threads` after its lookup.

`test_discord_create_not_resent.py::test_a_thread_create_keeps_its_retry` pins the current retry behaviour this follow-up builds on.

issues.title: claude backend: switch a live session's permission mode (auto -> bypassPermissions and back) from the dashboard, as Shift+Tab does in the TUI
issues.body:
## What

Let the user change a running dashboard chat's Claude Code permission mode — for example from `auto` to `bypassPermissions`, and back — without restarting the session, the way Shift+Tab cycles modes in the Claude Code TUI. A per-chat control (chat header or composer) that sends the mode change to the live backend session would cover it, ideally with an option to revert automatically at the end of the turn or task.

## Why

In auto mode, Claude Code's classifier denies some actions that the user has explicitly asked for, and the dashboard offers no way out of it mid-session:

- A bulk write to an external API that the user requested (a batch of `glab api graphql` mutations) was denied as `[External System Writes]`.
- Adding an allow rule through `/permissions` did not help: the rule only matches commands starting with `glab api graphql`, and the batch had to run as a script that calls glab, which the classifier denied again.
- Asking the agent to add the allow rule itself is denied as `[Permission Grant]`, which is correct, but leaves the user with no in-dashboard path.

In the TUI, the user presses Shift+Tab, approves once, and the work proceeds. In Kiro Crew the only workarounds are to paste the command after `!` themselves, or to leave the dashboard for a terminal session. Work that Claude Code can do today is blocked only by the dashboard's lack of a mode switch.

## Additional Context

- Backend: claude (Claude Code), dashboard chat, auto mode on.
- Related: #6812 (default approval mode for *new* sessions — this asks for switching a *live* one), #30169 (`KIROCREW_CC_PERMISSION_MODE=auto` starts in default mode), #12743 (classifier-approved calls bypass Crew's gate). A temporary `bypassPermissions` should still respect Crew's own deny floor and audit log, given #12743.
- Suggested labels for triage: enhancement, area: agents, area: dashboard.

issues.title: Artifacts: a folder PATCH with a null name renames the folder to None
issues.body:
## What happens

`PATCH /api/artifact-folders/{id}` with a body such as `{"name": null}` (or `{"name": null, "color": "#336699"}`) renames the folder to the text `None`.

`api_artifact_folder_update` (`src/kiro_crew/dashboard/handlers/artifacts_parts/artifact_folders.py`) tests `"name" in body`, which is true for a null value, and then passes `str(body["name"])` to `clean_name` and `rename`. `str(None)` is `"None"`, a valid non-empty name, so the folder is saved as `None` and a new emoji icon is generated for that name.

Create treats a null name as no name (`clean_name` turns `None` into an empty string and refuses it), so the two routes disagree.

## Expected

A null `name` in a PATCH leaves the folder name (and its icon) unchanged, while the other fields in the same body still apply.

issues.title: Computer Use on macOS reports a Cmd shortcut to a background app as sent, but it does nothing
issues.body:
## What happens

On macOS, `computer_press_key` with a Cmd shortcut (for example `cmd+a`) sent to an app that is not the frontmost app answers "sent cmd+a", but nothing happens in the app.

## Why

macOS delivers a Cmd shortcut to the frontmost app's menu bar and key window. A shortcut posted to a background app is dropped.

Measured on a Mac with TextEdit in the background and a terminal in front:

| Attempt | TextEdit | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `press_key cmd+a` | background | selection unchanged, tool said "sent cmd+a" |
| `AXPress` on Edit > Select All | background | press accepted, selection unchanged |
| set `AXSelectedTextRange` | background | all text selected |
| `press_key cmd+a` after TextEdit became frontmost | frontmost | all text selected |

## Expected

The tool does not report success for a key that cannot land. It refuses the Cmd shortcut when the target app is not frontmost, says why, and points the agent at element actions (`computer_click`, `computer_set_value`, `computer_perform_action`) instead. Plain keys such as Return and Tab are unaffected.

## Not in scope

Bringing the app to the front automatically. That takes the user's keyboard focus, so it needs its own opt-in and design.

issues.title: Evaluate Rust and MCU split to reduce OOMWOO compute requirements
issues.body:
# Issue draft: Evaluate Rust and MCU split to reduce OOMWOO compute requirements

## Context

OOMWOO currently targets Raspberry Pi 5 for the MVP compute module, while the
architecture still leaves open the question of "onboard ROS2 vs micro-ROS on an
MCU for the base controller".

Before the software stack grows, we should decide whether Rust can help reduce
CPU/RAM needs, and whether a split architecture could eventually let OOMWOO run
on cheaper or lower-power compute than Raspberry Pi 5.

This issue is **not** a proposal to rewrite OOMWOO in Rust. It is a proposal to
benchmark where language/runtime choices and MCU offload actually change the
hardware tier.

## Short hypothesis

Rust may help for small always-on custom nodes by removing Python runtime
overhead and improving memory safety, but it probably will **not** by itself move
the full MVP from Raspberry Pi 5 to a much smaller board if SLAM/Nav2 remain the
dominant CPU/RAM users.

The cost goal should be explicit: Rust is only a BOM reducer if it lets OOMWOO
move to a cheaper RAM/compute tier, avoid high-RAM Raspberry Pi 5 variants, or
remove enough Linux-side responsibility that a smaller SBC plus MCU becomes
viable. Otherwise it is mainly an engineering-quality choice, not a hardware-cost
reduction.

For a real compute reduction, the more promising direction is likely:

- SBC: ROS2, Nav2, SLAM, LiDAR processing, maps, high-level behavior
- MCU: motors, encoders, bumper/cliff/wheel-drop, e-stop, low-level safety,
  watchdogs, deterministic base control

Rust can still be useful in this architecture for selected host-side nodes, and
possibly for MCU firmware if the project chooses an embedded Rust stack. However,
micro-ROS itself is C/rclc-first today.

## Why this matters

If OOMWOO can run reliably on lower-cost/lower-power compute, the project gets:

- lower BOM cost
- lower battery draw and heat
- more headroom for future app-layer features
- smaller mechanical/thermal requirements
- better real-time behavior for safety and base-control loops

But the wrong optimization could increase contributor friction without reducing
the actual hardware requirement.

## Cost reduction angle

The practical question is not "is Rust faster than Python?" but "does the
architecture let us buy, power, cool, and package cheaper compute per robot?"

Snapshot from official product pages, plus one EU reseller example, checked or
provided on 2026-07-06:

| Hardware path | Cost signal | OOMWOO implication |
|---|---|---|
| High-RAM Raspberry Pi 5 | Raspberry Pi lists the 16 GB Pi 5 at $305; an EU reseller example from Elektor France lists the 16 GB board at EUR 144.95 incl. VAT, but out of stock. Pi 5 also recommends 5V/5A USB-C power and performs best with active cooling. | Treat high-RAM Pi 5 as a cost ceiling, not the default target. Avoiding high-RAM Pi 5 SKUs is a concrete savings goal, and price/stock must be recorded at benchmark time. |
| Lower-RAM Pi 5 / Raspberry Pi 4 | Pi 4 starts at $35 and offers 1/2/4/8 GB RAM variants with a 15W USB-C supply recommendation. | If measurements show OOMWOO can fit in 2-4 GB with headroom, the cost impact is much stronger than a small per-node optimization. |
| Compute Module 4 | CM4 starts as low as $41.25 and has 1/2/4/8 GB RAM options, but requires a carrier-board design. | Potentially attractive for a productized robot, but prototype savings can disappear once carrier board, connectors, and integration time are counted. |
| Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W | $15 board, 1 GHz quad-core Cortex-A53, 512 MB RAM. | Too small for full Nav2/SLAM unless the product scope changes, but useful as a bridge/lightweight side computer benchmark. |
| MCU + lower SBC | ESP32-S3-class MCU: dual-core 240 MHz, 512 KB SRAM, Wi-Fi/BLE, many GPIO/peripherals. | Strong candidate for motors, encoders, bumpers, cliff sensors, e-stop, watchdogs, and deterministic base control; not a replacement for onboard Nav2/SLAM. |

Cost should be measured as total compute BOM, not board price alone:

- SBC/module price at measurement time
- regional price and stock status, because reseller availability can be the
  difference between theoretical and real robot cost
- power supply/regulation requirement
- cooling requirement
- storage requirement
- carrier board or HAT requirement
- MCU/module, level shifting, cabling, and connector cost
- integration and maintenance cost from adding firmware, Rust, or micro-ROS

Useful cost-reduction hypotheses to test:

1. **Rust-only optimization:** saves memory on always-on custom ROS2 nodes; may
   matter only if several Python nodes are replaced and the whole stack fits a
   lower RAM tier.
2. **MCU offload:** likely stronger BOM impact because it can remove real-time
   control and safety I/O from Linux, simplify SBC responsibilities, and make a
   lower compute tier more realistic.
3. **Mapping/navigation split:** if MVP allows first-map generation on a dev
   machine and only navigation on the robot, onboard compute may drop
   significantly. This changes the product promise and should be explicit.
4. **High-RAM avoidance:** the clearest cost target is not "Rust everywhere"; it
   is "avoid needing 8-16 GB Raspberry Pi 5-class compute for the robot."

Cost success criteria:

- Worth it: measured OOMWOO workloads move from high-RAM Pi 5 to lower-RAM Pi 5,
  Pi 4/CM4, or lower-SBC-plus-MCU with enough RAM/CPU/thermal headroom.
- Worth it: MCU offload reduces Linux timing/safety risk and allows a cheaper
  SBC without hurting navigation reliability.
- Not worth it: Rust adds tooling/onboarding complexity but SLAM/Nav2 still
  force the same high-end SBC tier.
- Not worth it: CM4/MCU integration saves board cost but increases carrier-board
  or firmware maintenance cost enough to erase the robot-level savings.

## Compute-sensitive workloads

| Workload | Likely compute pressure | Language/runtime likely to matter? | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Gazebo simulation | Very high, dev-only | No | Not part of onboard robot compute. |
| SLAM / mapping | High | Low/medium | Mostly determined by algorithm, map size, LiDAR rate, and existing SLAM implementation. |
| Nav2 planning/control | Medium/high | Low/medium | Mostly C++ already; tuning matters more than rewriting custom glue. |
| LiDAR driver/filtering | Medium | Medium | Rust/C++ may help if custom processing grows. |
| Base motor control | Real-time sensitive | High if on SBC; better moved to MCU | MCU offload likely gives more benefit than host language choice. |
| Recovery/safety state machine | Low CPU, always-on | Medium/high | Good Rust candidate: small, safety-sensitive, latency/jitter-sensitive. |
| Job orchestration/status | Low CPU, always-on | Medium | Rust may reduce resident memory vs Python. |
| Home Assistant/app bridge | Low/medium | Medium | Depends on protocol stack; Rust could be efficient, but ecosystem matters. |

## Hardware tiers to evaluate

| Tier | Example | Fit for full MVP? | What must be true |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current target | Raspberry Pi 5 | Yes, expected | Enough for ROS2 + Nav2 + SLAM with headroom. |
| Lower SBC | Raspberry Pi 4 / CM4 | Plausible | Need measured SLAM/Nav2 performance and memory under OOMWOO maps. |
| Very small Linux SBC | Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W | Unlikely for full Nav2/SLAM | Could run simple bridge/control, but 512 MB RAM is likely tight for full ROS2 navigation. |
| MCU + SBC split | ESP32-S3 / STM32 + Pi class SBC | Strong candidate | MCU handles real-time I/O/safety; SBC handles planning/mapping. |
| MCU-only | ESP32-S3 / STM32-class | Not for MVP Nav2/SLAM | Only viable for non-ROS/simple vacuum behavior or as low-level controller. |

## Options to compare

| Option | What changes | Expected benefit | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keep Python/C++ ROS2 nodes | Use rclpy for glue, rclcpp/Nav2 for core robotics | Fastest development, strongest ROS2 contributor familiarity | Python always-on nodes may cost RAM and latency jitter. |
| Rust for selected ROS2 nodes | Reimplement small custom nodes using `rclrs` | Lower memory than Python, no Python runtime, stronger type/memory safety | `rclrs` is still rapidly evolving and has no stability guarantees; Jazzy setup is not yet as simple as rclpy/rclcpp. |
| C++ for selected performance nodes | Use rclcpp for custom performance-sensitive nodes | Mature ROS2 support, best Nav2 integration | More memory-safety risk than Rust; slower iteration than Python. |
| micro-ROS MCU base controller | Move low-level motors/sensors/safety to MCU | Better timing, less SBC responsibility, clearer safety boundary | micro-ROS is C/rclc-first; adds firmware and transport complexity. |
| Rust MCU firmware + ROS bridge | Use embedded Rust for MCU, bridge to ROS2 on SBC | Memory safety on MCU, explicit protocol | Not micro-ROS-native unless additional bridge work is done. |
| rmw_zenoh experiment | Keep languages, test Zenoh RMW | May help discovery/network behavior, especially multi-host | Does not directly reduce SLAM/Nav2 CPU. |

## Preliminary measurement

As a quick local reference, the current Python `oomwoo_recovery_safety` node from
PR #17 was started in the OOMWOO Jazzy Docker container and inspected after
roughly 8 seconds idle:

```text
RSS: ~53.7 MB
VSZ: ~616.9 MB
Process: python3
```

This is only an indicative measurement. It includes Python, rclpy, ROS2 runtime
overhead, and container environment effects. It should be repeated with:

- same machine
- same ROS domain/RMW
- warm and cold starts
- event burst load
- multiple samples
- Rust/C++ equivalents

Still, it gives a useful baseline: if several always-on Python nodes each cost
tens of MB RSS, replacing only selected nodes may matter on 1 GB / 2 GB systems,
even if it does not solve SLAM/Nav2 compute by itself.

## Proposed benchmark plan

### Phase 1: Baseline inventory

Run the current OOMWOO sim stack and record:

- process list
- RSS/PSS where available
- CPU while idle
- CPU during mapping
- CPU during navigation
- CPU during recovery event bursts
- startup time
- message latency from bumper event to `/cmd_vel`

Targets:

- Raspberry Pi 5, if available
- Raspberry Pi 4 / CM4, if available
- x86/ARM dev machine as reference only

### Phase 2: Language comparison for a small always-on node

Use `oomwoo_recovery_safety` as the benchmark because it is small, bounded, and
safety-relevant.

Implement/compare:

1. Python/rclpy baseline
2. Rust/rclrs equivalent
3. C++/rclcpp equivalent, optional but useful as mature ROS2 baseline

Metrics:

- RSS/PSS
- CPU idle
- CPU during 100/1000 trigger events
- p50/p95/p99 event-to-command latency
- p50/p95/p99 status publication latency
- cold-start time
- binary/package size
- build complexity
- contributor setup complexity

### Phase 3: MCU split experiment

Model low-level base controller responsibilities:

- wheel velocity command
- encoder odometry publication
- bumper/cliff/wheel-drop/e-stop publication
- watchdog: stop motors if host commands go stale
- local safety: e-stop and cliff stop must not depend on Linux scheduling

Compare:

- SBC-only base controller
- micro-ROS MCU base controller
- custom MCU protocol + ROS2 bridge

Metrics:

- host CPU/RAM reduction
- command latency and jitter
- odometry rate stability
- behavior during host crash or ROS graph restart
- firmware complexity
- recovery from serial/transport loss

## Decision criteria

Rust should be adopted for selected OOMWOO modules if it shows at least one of:

- materially lower RSS for always-on nodes compared with Python
- materially lower p95/p99 trigger latency or jitter
- simpler safety-critical state handling
- acceptable ROS2 Jazzy build reproducibility
- low contributor friction after templates/docs are added

Rust should **not** become the default if:

- Nav2/SLAM dominate CPU/RAM enough that custom-node language choice does not
  change the compute tier
- `rclrs` setup makes onboarding significantly harder
- a mature C++ node or micro-ROS/C firmware solves the same problem with less
  project risk

## Recommended near-term decision

1. Keep Python acceptable for prototypes and high-level glue.
2. Keep C++/Nav2 as the default for mature navigation/performance-critical ROS2
   integration.
3. Start a Rust experiment only for one small, always-on, safety-adjacent node:
   `recovery-safety`.
4. Treat MCU base-control split as the main path for reducing SBC requirements.
5. Do not aim for MCU-only OOMWOO while Nav2/SLAM are in scope.

## Concrete next action

Create a `compute-benchmark` contribution that contains:

- a script to launch one node and capture RSS/CPU/startup latency
- a Python baseline for `oomwoo_recovery_safety`
- a Rust/rclrs prototype with the same topic surface
- a small BOM sheet for each hardware tier, including board/module, power,
  cooling, storage, carrier/HAT, and MCU add-ons
- a short decision record after measurements

## Open questions

- What is the minimum acceptable target: Pi 5 only, Pi 4/CM4, or Pi Zero-class?
- Should the MVP require onboard SLAM, or can first-map generation run with a
  stronger dev machine while the robot runs navigation later?
- What is the expected map size and LiDAR update rate for the MVP demo?
- Should low-level safety be allowed to depend on Linux/ROS2 at all?
- Would maintainers accept Rust dependencies in the OOMWOO dev image?
- Should firmware be micro-ROS C/rclc, embedded Rust, or a minimal custom serial
  protocol with a ROS2 bridge?

## References

- OOMWOO architecture: Raspberry Pi 5 is the MVP compute target; onboard ROS2 vs
  micro-ROS MCU base control is still an open question.
- Raspberry Pi 5 official specs: Broadcom BCM2712 quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 at
  2.4 GHz, LPDDR4X RAM variants up to 16 GB, 16 GB model listed at $305,
  5V/5A USB-C power recommendation, and active-cooling recommendation under
  heavier use.
  https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-5/
- Elektor France Raspberry Pi 5 16 GB reseller example: contributor-provided
  snapshot on 2026-07-06 listed the board at EUR 144.95 incl. VAT and out of
  stock, illustrating why regional street price and availability should be
  recorded during benchmark/BOM work.
  https://www.elektor.fr/products/raspberry-pi-5-16-gb-ram?src=raspberrypi
- Raspberry Pi 4 official specs: starts at $35, RAM variants up to 8 GB, and
  15W USB-C power recommendation.
  https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-4-model-b/
- Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W official specs: 1 GHz quad-core Arm Cortex-A53 and
  512 MB SDRAM; official page describes it as a $15 computer.
  https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-zero-2-w/
- Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 official specs: starts as low as $41.25,
  Broadcom BCM2711 quad-core Cortex-A72 at 1.5 GHz, 1/2/4/8 GB RAM options, and
  eMMC/Lite storage options.
  https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/compute-module-4/
- Espressif ESP32-S3 official specs: dual-core Xtensa LX7 MCU at 240 MHz,
  512 KB internal SRAM, Wi-Fi/BLE, 45 GPIOs, and peripheral support.
  https://www.espressif.com/en/products/socs/esp32-s3
- `ros2-rust/rclrs`: Rust ROS2 client library with publishers, subscriptions,
  services, actions, QoS, parameters, logging, graph queries, timers, and
  executors; README notes that the client library is still rapidly evolving and
  has no stability guarantees.
  https://github.com/ros2-rust/ros2_rust
- micro-ROS: MCU-optimized rcl/rclc API in C; supports ROS concepts on MCUs,
  static memory pools, serial/UDP/Wi-Fi transports, and FreeRTOS/Zephyr/NuttX.
  https://micro.ros.org/docs/overview/features/
- `rmw_zenoh`: ROS2 RMW implementation based on Zenoh; useful for
  communication/discovery experiments, not a direct SLAM/Nav2 compute reducer.
  https://github.com/ros2/rmw_zenoh

Three scenarios cover Unicode edits, multiline joins, resize and rejected controls; all 17 steps pass locally. The native Edit suite also passes 82 tests plus 36 subtests.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Existing Python unit tests remain the main suite. The experimental interaction-check runner I maintain would only provide a shared JSON replay format. It does not test a terminal backend or replace the work in #1188.

**Additional context**
Urwid stays separately installed under its own LGPL license; no Urwid source is copied or relicensed. Would this be useful as an optional external example?

issues.title: agent mission create leaves a malformed scaffold when the target repo's pre-commit hook aborts
issues.body:
# Bug: agent mission create leaves a malformed scaffold when the target repo's pre-commit hook aborts

## Summary

If a repository's pre-commit hook aborts while `agent mission create` is committing, the command fails partway and leaves a scaffold that declares a coordination branch which no longer exists. The resume probe then reports `MISSION_RESUME_MALFORMED`, and the partial mission has to be removed by hand before a retry.

## Reproduction

Prerequisites: a repository with a `core.hooksPath` pre-commit hook that exits non-zero. The original occurrence was a hook that needed a Python with PyYAML, with no such interpreter available.

1. `spec-kitty agent mission create <slug> --topology coord ...`.
2. The hook prints `no usable Python interpreter — commit ABORTED` and the command fails.
3. Run the resume probe for that mission.

Expected: create rolls back fully, or leaves a state the probe can resume.

Actual: `kitty-specs/<slug>-<mid8>/meta.json` remains with `coordination_branch` set and `topology: coord`, the branch is gone, and the probe returns `MISSION_RESUME_MALFORMED`.

With the default `single_branch` topology the same abort leaves a scaffold the probe reports as `found`, so only the coordination-branch path is affected.

## Workaround Applied

Installed the repository's dependencies into its venv, saved a copy of the leftovers, removed the partial scaffold as the specify runbook prescribes, confirmed the probe returned `not_found`, and created the mission again. The retry received a new mission ID.

## Environment

spec-kitty-cli 4.0.0rc8 from PyPI via uv tool (tag v4.0.0rc8, commit 1d1a0c04c; the index artifact records no commit, so the installed SHA is unresolved), Linux. First seen on spec-kitty/spec-kitty @ `bcd2afa03` (git install), and reproduced on 4.0.0rc8 in a scratch repository. Repository with a custom `core.hooksPath`.

issues.title: Fresh consolidate lets a fully-canceled lane's content through when a dependency lane is re-approved over its merged commits
issues.body:
## Summary

A fresh `spec-kitty consolidate` (not a resume) may let a fully-canceled lane's content reach the target when a dependency lane is re-approved over that lane's merged commits. **This is a suspected gap, recorded from review reasoning. It needs a red test to confirm before any fix.**

## Where it was found

Mission `consolidation-window-provenance-01M6Y84D` (S1 #7403, PR #7490), in the reviews of WP05 and WP18. The record is `kitty-specs/consolidation-window-provenance-01M6Y84D/traces/design-decisions.md` on branch `feat/consolidation-window-provenance` (the WP18 entry for cell (g)), plus the S1 ADR residuals in the docs.

## The shape

- Lane A is approved. Lane C is fully canceled and depends on A. C's commits are merged into A.
- A is then re-approved over C's merged commits, so A's approval stamp covers them.
- The approved bound (`approved_bound.check_lane`) then has nothing to refuse, because a fully-canceled lane is neither an approval-stamp anchor nor a closed-world anchor.
- A fresh run on that state lets C's content through. The WP18 record says "a fresh run on the same state also lets C's content through (pre-existing fresh-run gap outside FR-015)".

Only this re-approved shape reaches the gap. When A advances after its approval and the lane is not re-approved, the bound refuses `LANE_MOVED_AFTER_APPROVAL`, with or without the frozen resume anchors (the WP05 and WP18 (g) pins record this, both green before and after #7490).

## Expected

Consolidation refuses, naming the canceled content (`CANCELED_REACHABLE_VIA_DEPENDENCY` or an equivalent), or the canceled content is excluded from what lands.

## Next step

1. Write a red-first test through the corpus harness (`tests/consolidation/test_reconciliation_intended_verdicts.py`, pin (g) documents both routes) for: A approved, C fully canceled and merged into A, A re-approved, then a fresh `consolidate`.
2. If it stays green, close this as not reproducible. If red, fix it in the gate or the attribution layer.

The WP18 record recommended a follow-up issue. Check the #7490 issue matrix before work starts; #7490 may have resolved part of this.

## Related

#7358 (gate soundness sub-epic), #7403 (S1), #7490, ADR `2026-09-29-1` (mixed-lane attribution), #5569 / #5613 (canceled-dependency content).

issues.title: Pin the decisions runtime lock end to end on coordination topologies and in lane worktrees
issues.body:
## Context

The #7493 fix makes the single_branch claim check ignore `kitty-specs/<mission>/decisions/index.json.lock` (#6628). It also stops `spec-kitty implement`'s planning auto-commit from staging the lock (`implement_cores.resolve_planning_artifact_staging`).

On a coordination topology (lanes / lanes_with_coord), the auto-commit fix is pinned only at unit level, with a fake GitPort (`test_coord_walk_never_offers_the_decisions_runtime_lock`). The pre-PR review of #7493 flagged this as a minor gap. It was deferred to keep that PR small.

## Gaps

1. **No end-to-end test on a coordination topology.** A CLI `spec-kitty implement` on a lanes_with_coord Mission with the lock present should assert that `git ls-files` lists no lock on the primary branch or the coordination branch.
2. **Lane-only dirty gates do not consult `is_decisions_runtime_lock`.** Each of these would refuse on the lock, or stage it, if the lock ever sat in a lane worktree. The decision service writes the lock on the placement surface, not in lane checkouts, so no reproduction exists today:
   - `_check_uncommitted_worktree_changes` (`cli/commands/agent/tasks_parsing_validation.py`)
   - `_validate_worktree_clean` (`lanes/worktree_allocator.py`)
   - the move-task lane auto-commit (`cli/commands/agent/tasks_move_task.py`)

   Confirm the lock cannot reach a lane checkout, then pin that, or exempt it.

Refs #7493, #6628, #5925

issues.title: doctor invocation-pairing can name the wrong work package as the orphan of a lifecycle group
issues.body:
## Symptom

`spec-kitty doctor invocation-pairing` names the latest `started` records of a lifecycle group as the orphans. It uses `invocation/lifecycle.py::unpaired_started` (or the inline slice that function replaced).

Pairing counts per `(mission_id, canonical_action_id)` group, and one `implement::implement` group holds every work package of a Mission. So when WP02's action completed and WP01's did not, the report can name WP02 as the orphan.

## Reproduce

In one checkout:
1. `write_started` WP01.
2. `write_started` WP02.
3. `write_paired_completion` for WP02.
4. Run `doctor_orphan_report`. It reports WP02 (the latest started record) as the orphan, not WP01.

## Context

Found by the WP02 reviewer of Mission `close-stale-lifecycle-records-01M72B89` (#7346), review cycle 3. That Mission's `doctor ops --close-stale` sweep already matches each completion to a started record of the same agent and work package first (`doctor/ops.py::_unpaired_ids`), so its closures name the right work package. The read-only report and `find_latest_unpaired_started`, which `next` uses to pair its own result, still use the latest-record label.

## Expected

The orphan report, and arguably `find_latest_unpaired_started`, pair by agent and work package first, as the sweep does. Counts per group are unchanged (C-004 of that Mission).

issues.title: dashboard: the folder-suggestion card offers a Bot's home folder, and Move silently does nothing
issues.body:
### Existing issues

- [X] I searched open issues and this is not already reported.

### KiroCrew version

0.12.0 (desktop app). Reproduced on that build. The code paths below are unchanged on `main` at `4697bd820db3`.

### Release channel

Stable

### How is it installed?

Desktop app

### Platform

Not platform-specific

### What happened

After a new session is titled, the folder-suggestion card ("Move this session to this folder?") appears above the composer. Clicking **Move** closes the card, but the session stays at the top level of the sidebar and no error is shown. It happened on two sessions in a row on 2026-11-10; both clicks are in the gateway's audit log (see below).

The suggested folder is a Bot's home folder. Since #25994, nobody but that Bot may file a chat into it, so the move can never succeed:

1. [`_eligible_folders`](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/blob/4697bd820db3934f20fc4b41b805ebdf07da2708/src/kiro_crew/dashboard/chat_folder_suggest.py#L77-L96) drops only `hidden` folders. A Bot's home folder and the folders inside it stay in the list that the project-directory match and the background model pick from. On an install whose only folder is a Bot's home, that folder is the only candidate.
2. [`FolderSuggestionCard`](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/blob/4697bd820db3934f20fc4b41b805ebdf07da2708/website/src/pages/chat/FolderSuggestionCard.tsx#L81) removes Bot folders from the dropdown, but [the fallback below it](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/blob/4697bd820db3934f20fc4b41b805ebdf07da2708/website/src/pages/chat/FolderSuggestionCard.tsx#L91-L93) adds the suggested folder back as the first option when the list does not contain it. The card shows the Bot's folder, preselected.
3. **Move** sends `PATCH /api/chat/slots/{slot}/folder`, which [`_refuse_mate_move_out`](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/blob/4697bd820db3934f20fc4b41b805ebdf07da2708/src/kiro_crew/dashboard/chat_folders.py#L131-L155) answers with 403 `mate_home_locked` ("this folder belongs to a Bot and is managed for you").
4. [`useMoveSlotToFolder`](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/blob/4697bd820db3934f20fc4b41b805ebdf07da2708/website/src/hooks/useMoveSlotToFolder.ts#L105-L112) rolls the optimistic move back without telling the user, and [`folderSuggestionAccept`](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/blob/4697bd820db3934f20fc4b41b805ebdf07da2708/website/src/pages/chat/page/followupCardActions.ts#L60-L64) clears the card in the same click.

**Expected:** a Bot's home folder, or a folder inside one, is never suggested. When every eligible folder belongs to a Bot, no card is shown.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Have a Bot whose home folder exists, and no other sidebar folder. Leave **Settings → Chat → Sessions → Folder suggestions** on (the default).
2. Start a chat with **New** and send a message on the same topic as the Bot's chats. Wait for the session to be titled.
3. The card asks "Move this session to this folder?" with the Bot's folder in the dropdown.
4. Click **Move**. The card closes and the session stays at the top level, with no error. The PATCH is answered 403 with `"code": "mate_home_locked"`.

It happens every time the model picks the Bot's folder. With no other folder on the install, that is any session on the Bot's topic.

Each step was checked separately on 0.12.0:

| Step | How it was checked | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1, 2 | Live gateway: the usage rows and the audit log (below) | The suggestion's model call ran for each session, and the card's **Move** PATCH followed 3 to 4 s later. The install's only folder is the Bot's home, so that was the only folder the card could offer. |
| 1 | `maybe_suggest_folder` run in-process from the shipped package against the real `folders.json`, with only the model reply stubbed to `1` | The prompt lists the Bot's home as its only folder, and a `slot_folder_suggestion` frame is sent for it. Nothing after the pick stops it. |
| 2, 4 | A throwaway vitest file rendering the real `FolderSuggestionCard`, `useFollowupCardActions` and `useMoveSlotToFolder`, with `api.setSlotFolder` rejecting with the gateway's message | The dropdown's only option is the Bot's folder, preselected. After **Move**, the session is filed optimistically, rolled back to unfiled when the call is refused, and the card is cleared. Nothing reports the refusal. |
| 3 | Live gateway: the same PATCH for a scratch session, sent through the `chat_folder_move_session` MCP tool | Refused with "this folder belongs to a Bot and is managed for you", recorded with the same caller and outcome as the card's clicks. The session stayed unfiled. |

### Relevant log output

```shell
# Usage rows (~/.kiro/crew/usage/tokens): the suggestion's model call
2026-11-10T02:23:39Z  slot=chat-56-1794277333  surface=bg:chat_folder_suggest
2026-11-10T02:25:14Z  slot=chat-57-1794277446  surface=bg:chat_folder_suggest

# Audit log (~/.kiro/crew/security_events.jsonl): the card's Move, a few seconds later
2026-11-10T02:23:43Z  PATCH /api/chat/slots/chat-56-1794277333/folder  outcome=error  caller=dashboard_user
2026-11-10T02:25:17Z  PATCH /api/chat/slots/chat-57-1794277446/folder  outcome=error  caller=dashboard_user

# The same PATCH for a scratch session, through chat_folder_move_session
chat_folder_move_session(session="chat-59-1794278569", folder="1448853d6426")
  -> Error: this folder belongs to a Bot and is managed for you
2026-11-10T02:43:27Z  PATCH /api/chat/slots/chat-59-1794278569/folder  outcome=error  caller=dashboard_user

# maybe_suggest_folder in-process (model reply stubbed to "1")
candidates shown to the model: ['1. <Bot display name> — (no sessions yet)']
frame sent: ('slot_folder_suggestion', '1448853d6426', '<Bot display name>')

# vitest, real card and hooks (website at 090dad8cf; these files are unchanged on main)
options = ["<Bot display name>"] selected = 1448853d6426
folder right after click = "1448853d6426" / after refusal = "" / card = cleared
```

The gateway log keeps WARNING and above, so the suggestion's own `Folder suggestion for slot …` INFO line is not recorded.

### Anything else

- Workaround: turn off **Folder suggestions**, or pick a folder of your own in the card's dropdown before clicking **Move**.
- #31604 (open) skips a Bot folder only in its new auto-apply mode (`refuses_write_into(state._folders, folder_id, "")` in `_file_into`). The default ask mode still sends this card.
- Suggested fix: in `_eligible_folders`, drop the ids returned by [`mate_home_subtree_ids(state._folders)`](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/blob/4697bd820db3934f20fc4b41b805ebdf07da2708/src/kiro_crew/dashboard/mate_folders.py#L141). That also covers the project-directory match, which reads the same list. A second guard in the card: render nothing when the suggested folder is Bot-managed, instead of adding it back.
- Out of scope here: a refused move reverts with no notice anywhere in the dashboard, not only on this card. #10910 set out to report that and was closed in favour of #10911, which covers offline writes only.

issues.title: Unable to reproduce MaskedMimic full-body tracking results from Table 1
issues.body:
Hi Chen!
  I am trying to reproduce the MaskedMimic full-body tracking results reported in
  Table 1 of the MaskedMimic paper using the provided SMPL checkpoint:

  ```text
  data/pretrained_models/masked_mimic/smpl/last.ckpt

  For MaskedMimic, Table 1 reports:

   Split          Success      MPJPE                                                                                                                                               
  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━
   AMASS Train      99.4%    32.9 mm
  ─────────────  ─────────  ─────────
   AMASS Test       99.2%    35.1 mm
  ```
  However, the evaluation results I obtain are much lower than these reported
  numbers.


  ## My understanding of the evaluation protocol

  Based on Section 7.2 and Section 8.1 of the paper, my understanding is:

  1. The deployable MaskedMimic prior should be evaluated, rather than the
     privileged posterior/encoder path.

  2. The model should use the mean of the prior latent distribution. Therefore,
     latent noise should be set to zero.

  3. For full-body tracking, all features of the future target poses should be
     visible to the model.

  4. Evaluation should be performed on flat terrain.
  5. A motion is considered failed if, at any frame, the average global joint
     position deviation exceeds 0.5 m.

  6. MPJPE should be reported in millimetres over global joint positions.

  Please correct me if any part of this interpretation is incorrect.

  ## Command used

  Due to the currently available configuration options on this branch, I used:

 ```text
  python protomotions/inference_agent.py \
    --checkpoint data/pretrained_models/masked_mimic/smpl/last.ckpt \
    --simulator isaaclab \
    --num-envs 256 \
    --motion-file data/amass/amass_smpl_test.pt \
    --full-eval \
    --headless \
    --overrides \
      agent.model.vae.vae_noise_type=zeros \
      agent.evaluator.evaluation_components.gt_error.static_params.threshold=0.50 \
      agent.evaluator.save_predicted_motion_lib_every=None
 ```

  My results are:
 ```text
============================================================
EVALUATION RESULTS
============================================================
  eval/action_delta_max_deg: 4.955446
  eval/action_delta_max_rad: 0.086489
  eval/action_delta_mean_deg: 0.837668
  eval/action_delta_mean_rad: 0.014620
  eval/action_rate_mean_rad_s: 0.438602
  eval/gr_error/max: 3.021279
  eval/gr_error/mean: 0.670585
  eval/gr_error/min: 0.030782
  eval/gt_error/failure_rate: 0.673913
  eval/gt_error/max: 4.850602
  eval/gt_error/mean: 0.368640
  eval/gt_error/min: 0.006625
  eval/high_jerk_frame_percentage_mean: 26.752044
  eval/max_joint_error/max: 5.211261
  eval/max_joint_error/mean: 0.679094
  eval/max_joint_error/min: 0.016715
  eval/normalized_jerk_mean: 1286.396362
  eval/num_evaluated: 138.000000
  eval/success_rate: 0.326087
  Items Evaluated: 138
============================================================
  Overall Score: 0.326087
============================================================
 ```
  These results appear to be far from the 99.2% test success rate reported in
  Table 1.



## Full-conditioning and posterior diagnostics

As an additional diagnostic, I evaluated both the prior and the privileged encoder-decoder/posterior policy under full conditioning. In both cases, all available future joint information was provided without masking, and the latent noise was set to zero.

### Prior with full future joint information

When the prior was given the full future joint information without any masking, it achieved a success rate of only **38.41%**:

```text
============================================================
EVALUATION RESULTS
============================================================
  eval/gr_error/max: 3.016995
  eval/gr_error/mean: 0.587996
  eval/gr_error/min: 0.031202
  eval/gt_error/failure_rate: 0.615942
  eval/gt_error/max: 4.020061
  eval/gt_error/mean: 0.294978
  eval/gt_error/min: 0.006706
  eval/max_joint_error/max: 4.543253
  eval/max_joint_error/mean: 0.559957
  eval/max_joint_error/min: 0.016551
  eval/num_evaluated: 138.000000
  eval/success_rate: 0.384058
  Items Evaluated: 138
============================================================
  Overall Score: 0.384058
============================================================
```

### Encoder-decoder/posterior with full future joint information

When the privileged encoder-decoder/posterior branch was evaluated using the full future joint information without any masking, it achieved a success rate of only **43.48%**:

```text
============================================================
EVALUATION RESULTS
============================================================
  eval/gr_error/max: 3.068513
  eval/gr_error/mean: 0.567266
  eval/gr_error/min: 0.030418
  eval/gt_error/failure_rate: 0.565217
  eval/gt_error/max: 3.617427
  eval/gt_error/mean: 0.289864
  eval/gt_error/min: 0.006679
  eval/max_joint_error/max: 3.932021
  eval/max_joint_error/mean: 0.550061
  eval/max_joint_error/min: 0.016800
  eval/num_evaluated: 138.000000
  eval/success_rate: 0.434783
  Items Evaluated: 138
============================================================
  Overall Score: 0.434783
============================================================
```

I understand that the privileged encoder-decoder/posterior policy is not necessarily equivalent to the paper’s independently trained fully constrained controller (FC). However, since the encoder branch receives the complete dense mimic target, I would still expect it to achieve a success rate above 90%, or at least perform substantially better than the prior.

The posterior branch improves the success rate only slightly, from **38.41%** to **43.48%**, and both results remain far below the values reported in Table 1. This makes me wonder whether there may be a mismatch in the checkpoint, motion data preprocessing, observation construction, target representation, or evaluation configuration.

## Questions

1. Could you please clarify why the provided MaskedMimic prior checkpoint achieves only a **38.41%** success rate under full conditioning, whereas Table 1 reports **99.2%**?

2. How should the similar performance of the prior and posterior be interpreted? In my evaluation, the posterior improves the success rate only from **38.41%** to **43.48%**, despite receiving the full dense target. I would appreciate any guidance on whether this behavior is expected or whether it may indicate a mismatch in the checkpoint, data processing, or evaluation configuration.

issues.title: SOMA23 on MuJoCo/Newton via ball joints: the stock FSQ tracker transfers, and a 25M-step decoder fine-tune closes the gap (follow-up to #256, #230)
issues.body:
Hi, following up on #256 and #230. Thanks for confirming the three-hinge vs. rotation-vector mismatch in #256. We needed the SOMA23 FSQ tracker on MuJoCo, so we built a ball-joint backend as subclasses outside the repo and measured it carefully. Sharing the results in case they help your fix; happy to open a PR or adapt to your design.

**Setup:** ProtoMotions `main` @ `7a8417a`; stock `motion_tracker/soma_bones_fsq`; BONES-SEED mini (61 clips). Evaluation on CPU MuJoCo 3.15; training on Newton 1.0.0 / warp 1.12.0 / mujoco-warp 3.5.0.2 on an NVIDIA L4. Tracked = the framewise mean body-position error stays ≤ 0.5 m over the clip (sampled actions, 30 Hz policy).

### 1. Ball joints instead of three hinges (CPU MuJoCo)
- **One ball joint per body.** Joint position = rotation vector of the parent→child rotation; joint velocity = child-frame relative angular velocity, i.e. what IsaacLab/PhysX report, so observations match training without remapping. The −X hinge axes on the left limbs drop out.
- **PhysX-style PD per axis on the rotation-vector error,** in the child frame, clipped per axis to the effort limit, with gains and limits from the robot config (incl. the anisotropic `RightForeArm` y damping, 80 vs. 30). Native armature (0.02), `implicitfast`, no MuJoCo actuators (torques via `qfrc_applied`).
- **Physics rate:** explicit PD needs ~1920 Hz (at 480 Hz it collapses: 0/48 on 16 hard clips × 3 seeds). Moving damping into MuJoCo's implicit `dof_damping`, with the explicit spring clipped so spring + damping stays within ±limit, works at **480 Hz: 25/48 vs. 26/48** at 1920 Hz explicit on those clips (4× cheaper; on all 61 clips, 1920 Hz tracked slightly more, 102 vs. 96 of 122, not significant).

**Stock tracker, no training, on this backend at 480 Hz** (all 61 clips × 5 seeds): **237/305 tracked** (45–48 of 61 per seed; IsaacLab 61/61). The three-hinge backend collapses within about 1 s on the same clips. Remaining failures: sharp turns and floor-contact clips (e.g. clip 20 fails on every seed).

### 2. Newton (MuJoCo-Warp) port: traps we hit
1. **The MJCF importer has no `type="ball"`** (non-hinge joints become prismatic). `add_mjcf(..., convert_3d_hinge_to_ball_joints=True)` on the stock SOMA23 MJCF gives the 22 ball joints with correct masses, inertias and armature; the backend doesn't pass this flag.
2. **Per-degree passive stiffness/damping:** the importer reads the MJCF's joint stiffness/damping as per-degree (about 57× too large). You already zero them; anyone adding implicit damping must write it back.
3. **Contact settings:** the backend's `geom_margin = geom_gap = 0.01` and `impratio = 10` differ from the MJCF's (0.001, 0, 1). Over 30 open-loop policy steps, Newton vs. CPU MuJoCo diverged 50–115 mm with the backend's settings vs. 2–5 mm with the MJCF's; with the backend's, our closed-loop runs went NaN within ~0.3 s.
4. **State conventions:** in SolverMuJoCo the free joint's linear `joint_qd` is the COM velocity and its angular velocity is world-frame; ball `joint_qd` / `joint_f` are child-frame. In our tests `eval_fk`'s `body_qd` didn't match the solver for ball joints, so we rebuild body velocities from `joint_q`/`joint_qd` (not isolated whether that's a Newton bug or our misuse).
5. **MuJoCo-Warp 3.5.0.2 damps ball and free joints with the first axis's damping** (`passive._spring_damper_dof_passive` reads `dof_damping[jnt_dofadr]` for every axis), while its implicit term and MuJoCo C use per-axis values. With 30/80/30 damping this is net anti-damping on y: a 5 rad/s kick grows without bound. It's fixed in MuJoCo-Warp `main`, and Newton `main` requires `mujoco-warp~=3.14`, so the fix is a pin bump in `requirements_newton.txt` once that works with the backend. Until then, a kernel swap: one-step parity vs. CPU MuJoCo goes from 3.2 mm / 1.0° worst case to ≤ 0.03 mm.
6. **Upstream skips the first policy update after every RESUME** (`train_agent.py`, "avoid training spike"). Fine, but worth documenting: our resume test failed until we accounted for it.

With 1–5 handled and our per-axis PD as a Warp kernel (written to `joint_f` each substep, inside your CUDA graph), Newton matches CPU MuJoCo on the 16 hard clips × 3 seeds: **27/48 on Mac CPU and 26/48 on the L4 vs. 25/48 CPU MuJoCo**. Throughput on the L4 at 480 Hz: ~8.3k env steps/s at 4,096 envs (8,192 runs out of memory).

### 3. Closing the gap: decoder-only fine-tune (one training run)
- **What trains:** only the FSQ **decoder and critic**, with PPO (`mimic/fsq.py` unchanged except a lower actor learning rate). The encoder, quantizer, actor normalisers and `logstd` are frozen; frozen tensors are verified bit-identical. Warm start from your `last.ckpt`; fresh optimizers.
- **Data:** the 16 hard clips only.
- **Length and cost:** **~25M steps, about one L4-hour.**
- **Evaluated on CPU MuJoCo, 61 clips × 5 fresh seeds:** **305/305 tracked** (stock 237/305); the 16 hard clips 80/80 (stock 40/80); clip 20 5/5 (stock 0/5); 0 regressions. The 45 clips excluded from fine-tuning also track at every seed.
- **Pushes** (root velocity kicks 0.5–2.0 m/s, 4 directions, 4 clips × 2 seeds): falls drop from **54/128 to 18/128**. Forward pushes are unchanged (22/32 survival both), so it's not uniformly better.
- **Caveats:** one training seed; the checkpoint was chosen after a development check; the mini set is within your tracker's training distribution. So this shows cheap adaptation to a new simulator, not generalization to unseen motions.

### What we can contribute
`BallMujocoSimulator` and `BallNewtonSimulator` subclass your `MujocoSimulator` / `NewtonSimulator`, plus a ~70-line Warp PD kernel with a numpy twin, the MuJoCo-Warp damping fix, and tests (state round trips, one-step parity, freeze/resume contracts). If useful, we can turn them into a PR, e.g. a ball-joint option for the SMPL-family robots with the Newton settings above, or just share the measurements and fixtures for your own implementation. The decoder fine-tune recipe works with your unchanged `train_agent`. Let us know which you'd prefer.

issues.title: [Feature]: public plugin API for per-account usage, pool entry identity, bench time and credential removal
issues.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Plugins that show per-account subscription usage (Claude / ChatGPT-Codex windows, which account is benched, which one Hermes moves to next) cannot do it through the documented plugin API today. The data and actions exist in core, but only behind names that `hermes plugins validate` flags as private (catalog rule 9):

| Need | Core symbol used today (not in `plugin_api.json`) |
|---|---|
| Read the per-account usage cache from backend code (and ask for a refresh) | `agent.account_usage_cache.cached_account_usage`, `snapshot_is_stale`, `refresh_account_usage_async`, `refresh_account_usage_entries_async` |
| A stable, non-secret identity per pool entry (to group the several credentials one Codex login creates, and to key per-account settings) | `agent.account_usage_cache._identity_id_for` |
| When a benched entry becomes usable again | `agent.credential_pool._exhausted_until` |
| Remove a credential with the same source cleanup `hermes auth remove` does | `hermes_cli.auth_commands.auth_remove_command` |

Concrete consumer: [plan-usage](https://github.com/ziadelboshy/hermes-plan-usage) (community plugin, catalog entry PR to follow). To stay inside rule 9 its public version reads usage through the Desktop `model.options` RPC and matches rows to pool entries by label, and it dropped account removal. Related: seeded pool rows (`claude_code`, `hermes_pkce`, `env:*`) in a named profile get a new random id on every `load_pool()`, so a plugin cannot key settings by entry id either; it falls back to `provider:source`.

### Proposed Solution

Add a small documented, read-mostly surface (names are suggestions):

1. `agent.account_usage.get_account_usage(provider, *, refresh=False) -> list[AccountUsageView]`: per pool entry, the cached snapshot (windows, resets, plan) plus `stale: bool`; `refresh=True` schedules the existing async refresh and returns the cached value.
2. `PooledCredential.identity` (or `credential_pool.entry_identity(provider, entry)`): the existing non-secret identity id, stable across loads and profiles.
3. `PooledCredential.benched_until: float | None` (public read of `_exhausted_until`).
4. `credential_pool.remove_entry(provider, entry_id) -> list[str]` running the same source cleanup as `hermes auth remove` and returning its notes, for an explicit user-confirmed action.

All four are thin wrappers over existing code; no new behaviour.

### Alternatives Considered

- Reading the Desktop `model.options` RPC from the desktop half (what plan-usage and `model-usage` do now): works for display, but backend code (warnings, logs, CLI) cannot use it, and label matching is ambiguous when two accounts share a label.
- Shelling out to `hermes auth remove`: interactive prompts and output parsing; not suitable for a plugin backend.

### Feature Type

Plugin API / extensibility

### Scope

Small: wrappers plus entries in `hermes_cli/data/plugin_api.json` and the public-API docs page.

issues.title: Validate paths in StateBackend methods for consistency and defense in depth
issues.body:
### Submission checklist

- [x] This is a feature request, not a bug report.
- [x] I searched existing issues and didn't find this feature.
- [x] I checked the docs and README for existing functionality.
- [x] This request applies to this repo (deepagents) and not an external package.

### Area (Required)

- [x] deepagents (SDK)
- [ ] dcode
- [ ] talon
- [ ] acp
- [ ] evals
- [ ] daytona
- [ ] modal
- [ ] quickjs
- [ ] runloop
- [ ] vercel
- [ ] langsmith-sandbox
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Feature description

For consistency and defense in depth, it would be useful to validate and normalize paths within the public methods of `StateBackend`, rather than relying exclusively on the validation performed by `FilesystemMiddleware`.

In typical usage, `StateBackend` is accessed through the built-in filesystem tools, which validate and normalize paths before passing them to the backend. However, custom tools running within the LangGraph execution context can also interact with `StateBackend` directly, bypassing that validation layer.

Consider an application where a custom tool fetches a file from an external API and stores it in the agent's state using the path returned by that API:

```python
@tool
def fetch_report_and_save_to_state():
    """Fetch a report and save it using the path returned by the API."""
    api_response = {
        "file_path": "../../dummy.md",
        "content": "# Dummy report",
    }

    backend = StateBackend()
    return backend.write(
        api_response["file_path"],
        api_response["content"],
    )
```

Since the backend is called directly, the path bypasses the validation normally performed by the filesystem middleware. As a result, a key containing a traversal sequence can be stored in the agent's state.

This can cause inconsistencies when the same file is subsequently accessed through the built-in filesystem tools, which do validate paths. For example, `read_file` rejects the traversal path, even though the file was successfully stored in the backend.

It can also affect applications that allow users to download files generated by an agent. A custom tool might retrieve files directly from the backend and materialize them in a local download directory:

```python
@tool
def download_state_file_to_local_directory(file_path: str):
    """Download a file from agent state and save it locally."""
    download_dir = Path("downloads").resolve()

    backend = StateBackend()
    response = backend.download_files([file_path])[0]

    if response.error or response.content is None:
        return f"Download failed: {response.error}"

    destination = (
        download_dir / response.path.lstrip("/")
    ).resolve()

    destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    destination.write_bytes(response.content)
```

If the stored path contains a traversal sequence such as `../../dummy.md`, using it to construct a local destination without an appropriate containment check can cause the file to be written outside the intended download directory.

Another example involves paths ending with a trailing slash. If a custom tool directly stores a file under a key such as `/reports/summary.md/`, `StateBackend.ls("/reports")` can interpret `summary.md` as a directory. Meanwhile, the built-in `read_file` tool normalizes the requested path before passing it to the backend, potentially making the stored file inaccessible through that tool.

These scenarios are relatively uncommon because `StateBackend` is typically accessed through `FilesystemMiddleware`. Nevertheless, validating and normalizing paths at the backend level would provide an additional layer of protection and ensure consistent behavior regardless of how the backend is accessed.

### Proposed solution (optional)

Reuse the existing `validate_path()` utility from `deepagents.backends.utils` to validate and normalize paths within `StateBackend` itself.

Apply this consistently across all public methods that accept file paths, including `ls()`, `read()`, `write()`, `edit()`, `delete()`, `grep()`, `glob()`, `upload_files()`, and `download_files()`.

This would ensure that paths are validated and normalized regardless of whether they reach the backend through the built-in filesystem tools or through direct calls from custom tools.

The validation already performed by `FilesystemMiddleware` should remain unchanged. Backend-level validation would provide an additional layer of protection rather than replace the existing one.

### Additional context (optional)

#### Related issues
- [#7167](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/7167?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — Related path-validation inconsistency in FilesystemBackend.

#### Reproduction
- [Python File](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34510828/repro.py): A runnable example demonstrating the behavior using an actual Deep Agents agent. It requires an OpenRouter API key, which is requested interactively at runtime.
- [LangSmith Trace (through their interface)](https://smith.langchain.com/public/67ca9b04-48a7-4a15-a8c9-5e7d078cf250/r/01a1b453-51e0-77a0-be9e-51e00a105210?start_time=2026-11-07T04%3A45%3A21.761248Z) / [LangSmith Trace (.json)](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34510870/trace-01a1b453-51e0-77a0-be9e-51e00a105210.json): Shows the agent executing the custom tools and the resulting behavior.

I'd be happy to work on an implementation if a maintainer is willing to assign this issue. 

Langchain 🪨s! 🦜

issues.title: feat(sdk): support rolling-window progress budgets for Nemotron Ultra
issues.body:
### Submission checklist

- [x] This is a feature request, not a bug report.
- [x] I searched existing issues and didn't find this feature.
- [x] I checked the docs and README for existing functionality.
- [x] This request applies to this repo (deepagents) and not an external package.

### Area (Required)

- [x] deepagents (SDK)
- [x] dcode
- [ ] talon
- [ ] acp
- [ ] evals
- [ ] daytona
- [ ] modal
- [ ] quickjs
- [ ] runloop
- [ ] vercel
- [ ] langsmith-sandbox
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Feature description

The built-in Nemotron 3 Ultra harness profile can prematurely terminate long-running, productive agent tasks because `NemotronProgressBudgetMiddleware` applies cumulative progress limits without considering elapsed time.

**Current behavior**

The middleware counts AI messages and tool results since the last external user message.

Once the history contains at least 16 AI messages or 48 tool results, subsequent model calls are short-circuited. Instead of continuing execution, the middleware returns a locally generated fallback response containing previously gathered results.

This can interrupt complex coding, research, and multi-step workflows even when the agent is making meaningful progress and sufficient context remains available.

The current safeguard does not distinguish between productive execution spread over time and excessive activity within a short interval.

This is an intentional harness-level protection, not a provider HTTP 429 error or context-window exhaustion.

**Reproduction**

Using synthetic message history and a fake model handler, request 20 progressing model calls within one user turn.

With the unmodified DCode 0.2.5 SDK profile, only the first 16 calls reach the handler. Subsequent attempts return the local budget fallback instead of continuing the pending operation.

**Requested enhancement**

Provide a configurable rolling-window progress-budget mode that:

- Limits the frequency of model and tool admissions rather than their cumulative lifetime within one user turn.
- Temporarily waits when a window is full.
- Automatically continues the pending operation once capacity becomes available.
- Preserves conversation history and completed tool effects.
- Retains independent runaway-loop protections.

The objective is to allow productive long-running tasks to continue without requiring another user message merely to reset a cumulative counter.

Because rolling-window pacing does not provide an equivalent total-cost safeguard, the existing behavior should remain available, preferably as the default.


### Proposed solution (optional)

A working local proof-of-concept patch for `NemotronProgressBudgetMiddleware` is available:

https://gist.github.com/tomtastisch/2a9102d0dc5e567689e18df511dacca7

**Implemented prototype**

The patch modifies the existing native middleware rather than introducing a second limiter.

It provides:

- Up to 60 model-call starts per rolling 30-second window.
- Up to 60 tool-call starts per separate rolling 30-second window.
- A 10-second wait-and-recheck loop when either quota is exhausted, continuing until a slot becomes available.
- Monotonic timestamps stored in bounded deques.
- Thread-safe, atomic admission using `threading.Lock`.
- Synchronous and asynchronous execution with cancellation support.
- Preservation of message history and completed tool effects.
- Single dispatch of each admitted operation without replaying previous tool effects.
- Retention of the existing three-consecutive-identical-tool-calls protection.
- No additional production dependencies.

Only admission timestamps expire. Message history, checkpoints, tool arguments, and previously completed operations are not removed.

The quotas apply to logical middleware admissions within an individual middleware instance. They are not distributed provider quotas and do not count every underlying HTTP retry.

**Upstream integration considerations**

The existing prototype directly replaces the default cumulative 16/48 limits with rolling 60/60 admission quotas. It does not yet implement an opt-in mode.

The existing `max_tool_results` constructor parameter is retained for compatibility, but its meaning changes from completed tool results to pre-dispatch tool admissions.

For upstream adoption, I recommend making rolling-window pacing explicitly configurable and preserving the original cumulative protection as the default, unless maintainers prefer another compatibility and cost-safety policy.

This would require a small adaptation of the prototype rather than submitting the existing patch as an unchanged default-behavior replacement.

**Suggested acceptance criteria**

1. Long-running productive turns can exceed the previous cumulative limits when rolling mode is enabled.
2. The 61st admission waits until a timestamp expires from its applicable window.
3. Concurrent calls cannot exceed the configured admission quota.
4. Sync/async cancellation prevents a waiting operation from being dispatched.
5. Existing history and completed tool effects are preserved.
6. Repeated identical tool calls remain protected.
7. Default behavior and total-cost implications are documented and covered by regression tests.

### Additional context (optional)

**Original issue**

https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/7615

The original issue was automatically closed because it was submitted programmatically. This submission uses the official GitHub Feature Request form.

**Source verification**

The cumulative limits are present in the Deep Agents SDK profile bundled with `deepagents-code==0.2.5` (`deepagents==0.7.34`).

Reference commit:

https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/efa9f5364b83e9367ea57d9c21b15b4d81fdcb7a/libs/deepagents/deepagents/profiles/harness/_nvidia_nemotron_3_ultra.py

The inspected upstream main branch also retains the cumulative 16/48 checks.

**Prototype and testing**

The published patch includes an SDK-only diff, a regression test suite, and documented verification results.

The supplied verification records report:

- Reproduction of the original cutoff: 16 of 20 progressing model calls reach the unmodified handler.
- 12 passing synthetic regression tests on the patched release profile.
- Coverage of rolling boundaries, independent quotas, concurrency, cancellation, retained history, and repeated-call protection.
- A scaled real-clock wait-and-continuation test.

These results were recorded in the supplied implementation package. They have not been independently reproduced in this review.

A complete DCode 0.2.5/Python 3.14 installation, current-main runtime testing, and live provider burst testing have not been established.

This contribution was prepared with AI assistance. I am willing to adapt the prototype into an SDK-only pull request after maintainer approval and assignment, following the repository's contribution guidelines.

issues.title: enable_gqa=True can be 2.59x slower than materializing the KV cache - silent MATH-backend fallback at decode
issues.body:
### Proposal to improve performance

Profiling a Llama-3.2-1B-shaped decoder (2048 hidden, 16 layers, 32 Q heads, 8 KV heads, 2048-token context) at decode time, I found a counterintuitive result and wanted to check it against this community's experience.
At batch 32, context 2048:
materialize KV with repeat_interleave then einsum: fastest
materialize then SDPA: 1.03x slower
enable_gqa=True (no materialization): 2.59x slower
Moving ~8x fewer bytes (34.36 GB/step down to the 4.29 GB logical cache) made it slower, because on this build no fused kernel accepts the grouped-query shape: flash-attn not compiled, mem-efficient and cuDNN attention runtime-disabled, so enable_gqa=True silently falls back to the MATH reference path. At decode the query length is 1, so attention is matrix-vector and the fused kernels that win at prefill either lose their edge or fail to qualify and fall back.
Is this expected on current builds, and is there a recommended way to detect the silent fallback programmatically? Measurement harness and numbers available.

### Report of performance regression

_No response_

### Misc discussion on performance

_No response_

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

```text
The output of `python collect_env.py`
```
